newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK June trade deficit seen widening.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK June trade deficit seen widening.

text.p: Britain's global trade deficit is expected to widen in June, reflecting an increase in the deficit in trade with countries outside the European Union to 1.127 billion stg, which was announced last month.

The Reuters consensus forecast is for a deficit on world trade in goods of 1.4 billion stg in June, up from the May shortfall of 985 million. July non-EU trade is expected to show a deficit of around 900 million stg.
The figures will be released on Wednesday.

"While the erratic short-term movements in the UK's trade balance always make estimation of the underlying trend difficult, recent data suggest that the whole-world goods deficit is broadly flat," said David Smith of Williams de Broe.
"This represents a not too discreditable performance given the weakness of demand in Britain's main EU trading partners and the relatively advanced stage of the domestic economic recovery."
Michael Saunders of Salomon Brothers expects trade with EU countries to show a gap of around 200 million stg, similar to the 171 million stg shortfall in May.
"We expect June's rise in the non-EU trade gap to reverse in July as June's dip in exports unwinds," he said.
"The trends of recent months have been for faster gains in exports to other EU countries, while imports from those countries have been flat."
Economists at UBS said the widening of the non-EU deficit in June was probably more indicative of the underlying trend than the narrowing of the whole-world trade gap seen in May.

"Tentative signs in the major business surveys of a pickup in export orders suggest that the recent pickup in export volume growth is likely to have been sustained in July," they wrote in a client note.
"But this is likely to have been offset by consumer-induced inflows of imported goods, leaving the deficit with non-EU countries broadly stable at 1.0 billion stg over the month."

Economists at Schroders said Britain appeared to have had some success in exporting into a depressed European marketplace, but this was unlikely to be sufficient to offset the widening in the June non-EU deficit.
The underlying trend in non-EU trade remains generally flat, they said.
